headline: Software and health-insurer selloffs leave every sector lower; tech and energy hold up best before Nvidia beats and guides above forecasts after the bell
summary: SPY fell 1.0% on Tuesday and this time the equal-weight RSP did worse (−1.4%) as the selling spread to banks, insurers and blue chips; over the past month SPY is still down 4.4% while RSP is up 1.1%. No sector rose: financials (−1.9%), utilities (−1.6%), communication services, real estate (both −1.5%) and health care (−1.4%) fell most, while energy and industrials (both −0.5%) and tech (−0.9%) lost least. Over the month health care (+5.5%), utilities (+5.0%) and staples (+4.9%) lead, and tech (−12.2%), energy (−6.5%) and communication services (−4.4%) lag. Behind it: an AI-disruption sell-off in software a day before Anthropic's IPO prices, a proposed Medicare Advantage audit rule that hit insurers, and a hawkish Fed speaker keeping a December hike priced, with the 10-year at 5.10%.
drivers: Software, not chips, led tech lower

Salesforce fell 9.5% and Intuit and ServiceNow about 7% on AI-disruption fears, but chips steadied and XLK lost only 0.9%. After the close Nvidia reported $115.8bn of revenue (about $109bn expected) and guided Q4 to $130bn ±3% (about $125bn expected), with gross margin guided down to 71–72%; the stock rose 2–5% after hours. XLK goes into Wednesday at RSI 27 and 12.3% below its 50-day average.
A Medicare audit proposal hit health care

CMS's proposed CRUSH anti-fraud rule would widen Medicare Advantage risk-adjustment audits; CMS puts recoveries at about $9bn a year. UnitedHealth fell 5.4% and Humana about 4%, taking XLV down 1.4%, though it remains the best sector over a month and 16.0% above its 200-day. Comments are due Jan 19, 2027.
Breadth gave way, and financials led the losses

The equal-weight index fell more than SPY for the first time since Nov 12. JPMorgan lost 2.4% after naming a new CFO and XLF fell 1.9%, while Home Depot (−2.5% on a soft outlook and CEO change) and Nike (−6.3%) weighed on discretionary despite October retail sales in line (+0.2%) and a firmer control group (+0.6%).
Strategists keep repricing sector calls for 2027

Wells Fargo set an 8,200 end-2027 target, cut staples to underweight and financials and industrials to equal weight, and raised discretionary and communication services to overweight; it sees accelerating earnings in hyperscalers and health care as long as the 10-year stays below 5.25%. Barclays (8,700) upgraded health care, and Morgan Stanley (8,700) keeps industrials as its top sector.
rotation: The rotation map is unchanged again: tech in Lagging, energy in Weakening, communication services in Improving, and the other eight sectors in Leading, largely because tech's slide lifts everything else relative to SPY. No sector changed quadrant since Monday. XLK's 3-month relative strength improved slightly to −6.5 points (from −7.8) as it fell less than the index, while health care (+10.4 points) and staples (+10.9) gave back some ground. Materials slipped to 0.2% below its 200-day, the first Leading sector to lose its long-term trend. The rotation ends if XLK holds Tuesday's level after Nvidia's beat, then reclaims its 50-day average (12.3% above the price) with creations continuing; a fade of the after-hours gain would keep the defensive leadership intact.
flows: State Street flows (to Nov 16) show dip-buying in tech accelerating: XLK took in $638m in a week, $2.47bn in a month (2.2% of assets) and $3.60bn over 3 months while its price fell 12.2% in a month, so ETF holders are not washed out and Nvidia's reaction matters. Health care added $1.19bn (2.4% of assets) in a month and materials $294m, the largest relative inflow at 3.5% of assets. Utilities lost $1.79bn (7.5% of assets) despite a 5.0% monthly gain, and communication services $958m (4.4%), so both rallies lack ETF sponsorship. Staples drew $715m in the latest week, chasing the defensive bid, and financials $304m, though XLF is still down $3.25bn over 3 months near its highs. For scale, SPY took in $7.08bn in the week and $654m over the month (0.08% of its $0.79tn).
model: The six-factor model (12-1 month momentum 25%, 3-month relative strength 20%, trend vs the 200-day 15%, 1-month flows as % of assets 15%, forward P/E vs the S&P 500 15%, latest-quarter EPS growth 10%) ranks energy first (82), health care second (68), then staples (57), materials (55) and financials (51); communication services is now alone in last (31) behind utilities (33). Tech moved up to sixth (50) and real estate slipped to seventh (47). Energy's lead rests on 12-month momentum (+52%), valuation (12.2x) and 151% Q3 earnings growth, all slow inputs, while its price is down 6.5% in a month with RSI 33. Health care earns its rank on relative strength (+10.4 points), trend (+16.0%) and inflows. I differ on energy (neutral, as the oil tape is still weak), financials (overweight, reading 3-month redemptions as under-ownership) and tech (more constructive than sixth, given Nvidia's beat, oversold conditions and steady creations).
weightsSrc: Schwab Center for Financial Research, as of Oct 2, 2026; rolled forward by each sector ETF's price change

XLV.view: Still the cleanest leadership: the best 1-month return of any sector (+5.5%) and earnings that don't hinge on AI capex. Tuesday's 1.4% drop came from managed care after CMS proposed wider Medicare Advantage audits (UnitedHealth −5.4%), a headline risk for insurers rather than pharma or tools. Barclays upgraded health care this week and Wells Fargo sees its earnings growth accelerating, though it flags overbought sentiment.
XLV.modelView: Second (68): +10.4 points of 3-month relative strength, the strongest trend (16.0% above the 200-day) and inflows worth 2.4% of assets in a month. Weak spots are 9% Q3 earnings growth in the model's input and a soft latest week ($69m out).
XLV.trade: Hold the overweight; add on a pullback towards the 50-day average (now 5.5% below the price), favouring pharma and tools over managed care until the CRUSH rule is clearer.
XLV.risk: The audit rule widening into a broader Medicare Advantage squeeze; a sharp tech rebound pulling money out of defensives.

XLF.view: A 10-year yield above 5% supports bank margins and capital-markets activity is strong; at 15.1x forward earnings the sector is about 83% of the market multiple. XLF was the worst sector on Tuesday (−1.9%) as JPMorgan fell 2.4% on a CFO change and breadth gave way. Wells Fargo cut financials to equal weight in its 2027 outlook, while Morgan Stanley still sees select opportunities in the group.
XLF.modelView: Fifth (51): +4.2 points of 3-month relative strength and 6.3% above the 200-day, held back by flows ($589m out in a month, $3.25bn over 3 months). The model scores that as a negative; I read it as under-ownership, and $304m came back in the latest week.
XLF.trade: Overweight; prefer large money-centre banks and brokers over regionals, and add if XLF holds above its 50-day average (2.0% below the price).
XLF.risk: Private-credit or commercial real estate losses; a flatter curve if the Fed over-tightens.

XLK.view: Nvidia's first report under an interim CEO beat: $115.8bn of revenue and a $130bn Q4 guide, both above forecasts, though gross margin is guided lower and the guide excludes China. Before that, software fell hard on AI-disruption fears (Salesforce −9.5%), so the sector's problem is now as much software as chips. XLK is −12.2% over a month with RSI 27 and still earned 69% Q3 earnings growth at a forward P/E below the market's.
XLK.modelView: Sixth (50), up one place: second-best 12-month momentum (+30%) and strong valuation, earnings and flow scores (+2.2% of assets in a month) offset the worst 3-month relative strength (−6.5 points) and a price 4.4% below the 200-day.
XLK.trade: Build back towards benchmark in thirds: the first tranche on Nvidia's beat is due, the second on a close back above the 50-day average, the third on a retest of the low that holds.
XLK.risk: Nvidia's after-hours gain fading and dip-buyers in the ETF capitulating; software de-rating further on AI disruption.

XLP.view: Staples fell 1.2% on Tuesday but are +4.9% over the month on a safe-haven bid. At 23.7x forward earnings they cost about 30% more than the market, and Wells Fargo cut the sector to underweight in its 2027 outlook. Walmart's results on Thu Nov 19 are the next test.
XLP.modelView: Third (57) on strong 3-month relative strength (+10.9 points) and trend (8.7% above the 200-day), with a weak valuation score. ETF buyers arrived late: $715m in the latest week, but still $138m out over a month.
XLP.trade: Neutral; trim into strength near RSI 65–70 and rotate into health care, a similar defensive with more growth.
XLP.risk: A deeper growth scare would extend the defensive bid.

XLE.view: The cheapest sector (12.2x) with the fastest earnings growth (151% in Q3 per FactSet) and still +44.5% this year. Crude steadied on Tuesday (WTI +0.3% to $86.01, Brent $93.14) on tanker attacks in Hormuz, but Brent is down 20% this month on surplus forecasts and XLE is −9.5% month to date. Wells Fargo lifted energy to equal weight.
XLE.modelView: First in the model (82) on valuation, earnings and 12-month momentum (+52%), but the near-term inputs are weak: RSI 33, −6.5% over a month, Weakening on the rotation map and only $56m of creations in a month. That is why I hold neutral rather than following the model's overweight.
XLE.trade: Hold at neutral as a hedge against Middle East escalation; add only if WTI holds the mid-$80s and XLE regains its 50-day average.
XLE.risk: Further surplus-driven oil weakness; escalation is the upside risk.

XLB.view: Materials are +13.6% this year on copper, gold and data-center demand, with about 30% Q3 earnings growth (FactSet). But the sector fell 3.8% in a week and slipped just below its 200-day average, with the dollar strong and gold weak.
XLB.modelView: Fourth (55): the largest relative inflow of any sector ($294m, 3.5% of assets in a month) and a positive 20-day money flow (CMF +0.10), but the trend is now 0.2% below the 200-day and 3-month relative strength only +1.8 points.
XLB.trade: Neutral; prefer copper and data-center materials over chemicals, and wait for a close back above the 200-day before adding.
XLB.risk: A stronger dollar and slower China demand.

XLC.view: Down 9.8% this year and below its 200-day as investors question returns on Meta's and Alphabet's AI spending; FactSet shows the sector had the largest negative Q3 earnings surprise, though earnings still grew about 18%. At about 18x forward earnings it is no longer expensive, and Wells Fargo upgraded it to overweight for 2027.
XLC.modelView: Last (31), now alone: flat 12-month momentum, 5.8% below the 200-day and $958m of outflows in a month (4.4% of assets). Valuation is the only positive; it sits in Improving on the rotation map.
XLC.trade: Neutral; a bounce candidate if tech turns, but it needs to reclaim its 200-day average first.
XLC.risk: More capex without matching revenue; advertising slowing if the consumer weakens.

XLI.view: Industrials are down 9.2% over three months as the AI-power equipment trade unwound and trade at 22.5x forward earnings, a premium to the market. The split among strategists is wide: Morgan Stanley's top sector for 2027, while Wells Fargo just cut it to equal weight. It held up best on Tuesday (−0.5%), helped by Nvidia nerves easing.
XLI.modelView: Ninth (36): −4.7 points of 3-month relative strength, 4.7% below the 200-day and a poor valuation score. Flows are improving, with $549m of creations in the latest week.
XLI.trade: Underweight; keep aerospace and defence, and revisit electrical equipment only on a close back above the 200-day.
XLI.risk: A fast AI-capex rebound after Nvidia would lift the electrical-equipment names first.

XLY.view: Discretionary is up 2.3% over the month but down 1.3% this year and at 25.1x forward earnings is the most expensive sector (FactSet). Home Depot (−2.5% on a soft outlook) and Nike (−6.3%) weighed on Tuesday even though October retail sales held up. Wells Fargo upgraded the sector to overweight, the main argument against my underweight.
XLY.modelView: Eighth (39): flat 12-month momentum and the weakest valuation score; +3.5 points of 3-month relative strength, with $246m in the latest week but $131m out over a month.
XLY.trade: Underweight; fade the bounce unless Walmart (Nov 19) and holiday data surprise to the upside.
XLY.risk: A strong holiday season or a Tesla-specific rally.

XLU.view: Utilities fell 1.6% on Tuesday but are +5.0% over the month as a haven. A 10-year yield at 5.10% competes with their dividends and XLU has lost $1.79bn in a month. Morgan Stanley is overweight on power demand; BNP Paribas prefers to wait for clarity on data-center regulation and power-price caps.
XLU.modelView: Tenth (33): weak 12-month momentum and the worst flow score (−7.5% of assets in a month), with RSI 62 and the price 1.1% below the 200-day.
XLU.trade: Underweight; use haven bounces to reduce.
XLU.risk: A bond rally if the Fed turns dovish, or a sharper risk-off move.

XLRE.view: The most rate-sensitive sector, and the Fed is still expected to hike in December. It fell 1.5% on Tuesday but is +4.6% over the month; office and retail still face refinancing at much higher rates.
XLRE.modelView: Seventh (47), down one place: +2.2 points of relative strength, a positive 20-day money flow (CMF +0.11) and $112m of creations in a month, but weak 12-month momentum and no valuation input.
XLRE.trade: Underweight the sector; prefer data-center and health-care REITs if exposure is needed.
XLRE.risk: A fall in long yields would spark a sharp short-covering rally.
